newsitem.title: HONG KONG: List grows for Hong Kong leadership hopefuls.
newsitem.headline: List grows for Hong Kong leadership hopefuls.

text.p: Two shipping tycoons, two former judges and a top woman civil servant are among the contenders to be Hong Kong's first post-colonial chief executive when China reclaims the territory from Britain next July 1.
But rather than any popular election, the successor to Governor Chris Patten will be chosen by a 400-member selection committee named by China. A decision is expected by the end of this year.
Here are sketches of five frontrunners and one who is the public's favourite but has not declared her candidacy.

TUNG CHEE-HWA - A Shanghai-born shipping tycoon, Tung, 59, is an ex-member of the governor's advisory Executive Council. He heads the Orient Overseas (International) Ltd shipping group and is a vice-chairman of the China-handpicked Preparatory Committee on the handover. He has strong contacts with China, Taiwan, Britain and the United States. Widely seen as Beijing's favourite, Tung announced his interest in the chief executive contest two weeks ago. He has yet to reveal his policy goals for Hong Kong's future.

A recent poll by the Hong Kong Economic Times gave Tung 55 percent of public support, but this excluded Anson Chan, who is not a candidate but is Hong Kong's most popular political personality. It also excluded former business executive Peter Woo, who had not declared his candidacy at the time.

SIR TI LIANG YANG - China-born Yang, 67, resigned as Hong Kong's Chief Justice last month to run for the top job. He was knighted in 1988, when he became the first Chinese to head the Hong Kong judiciary under British rule. Yang's family moved to Hong Kong from Shanghai after the 1949 communist takeover. He is unpopular with the pro-democracy camp for remarks last year in which he attacked a Bill of Rights introduced by Patten against China's will.
The opinion poll showed Yang with 37 percent of popular support, behind Tung.

PETER WOO KWONG-CHING - Shanghai-born tycoon Woo, 50, is a son-in-law of late Hong Kong shipping magnate Sir Yue-kong Pao. The youngest candidate, he is honorary chairman of Wharf (Holdings) Ltd and Wheelock and Co Ltd, but no longer engages in day-to-day running of his companies. He is chairman of Hong Kong's Hospital Authority. This week, Woo was the first among the potential candidates to declare a policy platform, vowing to protect Hong Kong's fiscal policies and financial system after the handover. Hong Kong media expressed the view that Woo's policies would inevitably be affected by his business links.
Woo did not figure in the poll, taken before he declared.

ARTHUR GARCIA - A retired Hong Kong High Court judge and ombudsman, the 72-year-old Garcia said last week he was considering a run for chief executive. Born in Hong Kong of a Chinese mother and Portuguese father, Garcia is a member of the Preparatory Committee working out details of the handover. Garcia's bid came as a surprise. He said he had sufficient experience from his career to know how government machinery worked. Garcia did not figure in the poll.

ANSON CHAN FANG ON-SAN - Shanghai-born Chan, aged 56, is Hong Kong's Chief Secretary, the most powerful civil servant and deputy to Governor Patten. The first woman to reach this post, the no-nonsense "iron lady" with a big smile is respected by civil servants after 34 years in government service. British officials let it be known they would love to see her as chief executive, and she has said she would like to continue to serve Hong Kong. She has steered clear of quarrels with China, and is respected in Beijing, but her strong links to the Patten establishment work against her chances.
Chan was not included in the latest poll, but earlier polls consistently showed her as the public's favourite when measured against Tung and others.

LO TAK-SHING - Oxford-educated Lo, 61, a lawyer and adviser to Beijing, was born in Hong Kong to one of Hong Kong's oldest Eurasian merchant families. He is a former member of the legislature and the governor's Executive Council and a member of the Preparatory Committee. Lo stirred controversy last year by saying he was renouncing his British passport for a Chinese one. He also aroused hostility in the media by saying that if he ran Hong Kong, journalists who write "anti-constitutional" articles would be arrested.
The opinion poll showed Lo with eight percent support.
